source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Three principles define the framework. (1) Cognition is split into an object level and a meta level. (2) The meta level holds a dynamic model of the object level. (3) Two relations differ by direction of information flow: control (meta to object) and monitoring (object to meta).
numbers: Principle 2 rests on Conant and Ashby (1970): a controller needs a model of what it controls. Figure 1 contrasts the real system with three non-meta designs: no feedback, monitoring without control (a spy), and a symmetric pair.
quote: the opposite does not occur, i.e., the object-level has no model of the meta-level.
limits: Two levels only; the authors say more levels are possible but not needed. The object level has no model of the meta level.
agent_relevance: Our S6 split matches this: code is the meta level and holds the state model; the model is the object level and has no model of the code. Asymmetry is the design, not an accident.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Control changes the object level: it starts, continues or ends an action. Monitoring only informs the meta level. Because control gives no information back, a monitoring channel is needed and is logically independent of control.
numbers: Telephone-handset analogy: control is speaking, monitoring is listening.
limits: Logical independence is claimed, not always psychological independence.
agent_relevance: In S6 code must have both channels: a signal in (monitor) and a lever out (operator choice, stop, continue). A loop with only one is not a controller.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Introspective reports are treated as data to be explained, not as a true view of internal processes. People are imperfect measuring devices of their own cognition, and even distorted monitoring still drives control.
numbers: Telescope analogy: study the instrument and its distortions, not only the sky. Cites Nisbett and Wilson (1977) and Ericsson and Simon (1980, 1984).
quote: introspection can be examined as a type of behavior so as to characterize both its correlations with some objective behavior
limits: This is a methodological stance. It does not say how large the distortions are.
agent_relevance: Matches our guardrail G10: a model's own report about itself is a signal with known bias, never evidence. Use it as input to a code rule, and score it against outcomes.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: The framework is laid out by stage: acquisition (before learning, ongoing), retention, retrieval. Monitoring judgments sit above the stages and control decisions below. Ease of learning (EOL), judgments of learning (JOL), feeling of knowing (FOK) and retrospective confidence are the monitoring types.
numbers: Control types: choice of processing, allocation of study time, termination of study, choice of search strategy, termination of search, and output of the response. Prospective monitoring: EOL (before learning), JOL (recallable items), FOK (non-recallable items). Confidence is retrospective.
limits: Fig. 2 is a skeleton. The authors refine nodes in later figures (Fig. 4 acquisition, Fig. 5 retrieval) using a coarsening and refining scheme, with no fixed lowest level.
agent_relevance: Gives us a clean table of monitor-signal and control-action pairs to copy for S6: each monitor type should have one named control it feeds.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Study-termination rule (Fig. 4): the learner compares the current state of mastery (from a JOL or FOK) with the norm of study (the wanted mastery). If mastery is below the norm, the learner allocates more time and picks a strategy from a metacognitive library. If it reaches the norm, study ends.
numbers: Norm of study = wanted ease of retrieval at test, raised by the person's theory of retention over the delay. The strategy library stores an estimated acquisition rate per strategy and item kind.
limits: A hypothesis model, drawn as a box diagram. Not fitted to data in this chapter.
agent_relevance: This is a discrepancy-reduction loop and a direct template for S6: goal level, measured level, gap, then pick the strategy with the best expected rate. Code can compute all four; the model supplies only the attempt.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Retrieval-termination rule (Fig. 5): a very fast preliminary FOK decides whether to search at all. During search an ongoing FOK and a cost-reward rule decide whether to continue. If FOK falls below threshold, search ends with an omission. A found answer is output only if confidence passes a threshold, which may drop with time (test until deemed successful) or be set by satisficing.
numbers: Cites Simon (1979) satisficing. Drug evidence: marijuana raises commission errors without changing correct recall; high altitude (Nelson et al. 1990) lowered commission errors without changing correct recall.
limits: The output threshold and the search threshold are separate parameters. Evidence for the drug effects is from other papers summarised here, not re-run.
agent_relevance: Two separate thresholds, one for effort and one for answering, map onto our S6 stop-rule and S7 select-rule. Do not use a single confidence number for both.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Early finding: feeling-of-knowing rankings were highly reliable but nearly invalid. People ranked items the same way on retest, and transitively, yet the ranking did not predict later recognition. The authors called it a fun-house mirror.
numbers: First experiment 1976, number-word pairs, paired-comparison rankings, replicated in unpublished experiments 1977 to 1979. Retest reliability near perfect (Nelson, Leonesio, Landwehr and Narens 1986, Fig. 2).
limits: Unpublished at the time. Rejected explanations: people are inherently poor monitors; forward and backward traces differ.
agent_relevance: A stable self-rating is not a valid one. Test any model self-score for validity against outcomes, not only for consistency across reruns.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Monitoring accuracy depends on how well the item was learned, not on retention interval or recall level. FOK accuracy was nil after one correct recall and clear after four.
numbers: 1979 experiment, 3 groups, n = 27 or 28 each: immediate test after one study trial, 35% recall, 63% of subjects with positive gamma (not significant); 1 week after one correct recall, 45% recall, 71% positive (marginal); 3 weeks after one correct recall, 25% recall, 86% positive (p < .001). 1980 experiment: 1 week, one correct recall: 29% recall, mean G = +.15; 4 weeks, one recall: 15%, G = +.14; 4 weeks, four recalls: 38%, G = +.36. Published version (Nelson, Leonesio, Shimamura, Landwehr and Narens 1982, 4 weeks): median G = .00 for one recall, +.41 for four.
limits: Group differences in recall level cannot explain the result (the first group was bracketed). Exact N for 1980 groups not given.
agent_relevance: Monitoring only works on material with enough trace. For our agent: self-assessment on a problem the model barely represents will be near chance, so route those cases to external checks, not self-ratings.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Mechanism for the overlearning effect: a judgment can only separate items that differ. Overlearning raises the spread between easy and hard items, so judgments become more accurate. Low gamma may mean low item spread, not a poor monitor.
numbers: Leonesio and Nelson (1982): gamma between trials to first correct recall and later retention was +.02 (criterion one recall), -.15 (two) and -.25 (four). Leonesio (1985): FOK-recognition G = +.28 fell to +.01 once item difficulty was partialled out. Nelson, Leonesio et al. (1986): FOK G = .00 for items adjacent in rank, +.77 for top versus bottom items.
quote: a low value of G does not necessarily imply that the task is insensitive or that the person cannot monitor accurately
limits: Correlational. Partialling shows difficulty carries the effect in that sample.
agent_relevance: When we measure monitor accuracy for our agent, report it with the spread of item difficulty. A flat benchmark will make any confidence signal look useless. Pair items far apart in difficulty.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Different monitoring judgments are not one signal. EOL, JOL and FOK correlate only weakly, and they predict later recall differently.
numbers: Leonesio and Nelson (1990): later recall predicted by JOL with G = +.31 and by EOL with G = +.12. EOL predicted number of trials to learn with mean G = -.22; trials predicted recall 4 weeks later with G = -.48. JOL made 4 weeks earlier predicted recognition of non-recalled items as well as an immediate FOK. Overlearning raised JOL more than later FOK (Fig. 8).
limits: Sample sizes not given in the chapter.
agent_relevance: Do not average an LLM's pre-task difficulty guess, mid-task progress guess and post-hoc confidence into one score. Keep them as separate inputs, each with its own validity.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: FOK misses new information. A brief flash of the correct answer raised recall but not the feeling of knowing, so FOK reads only what is already in memory.
numbers: Jameson, Narens, Goldfarb and Nelson (1990), Table I. Experiment 1: p(recall) .28 after correct-answer flash versus .10 after nonsense; FOK 5.4 versus 5.2 (not significant). Experiment 2 (FOK without recall attempt): 6.1 versus 6.1.
limits: Sample sizes not given. Authors leave open whether flashed information sits in STM or unconscious memory.
agent_relevance: A monitor can lag a fresh input: after a new hint or tool result the model's own confidence may not move though its answer changes. Re-check with code after new input; do not trust the old rating.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Privileged access is real but modest. For predicting a person's own later recognition, the person (Target) beat an outside Judge who saw only the question; an Observer who watched the recall attempt fell between them.
numbers: Two experiments, 15 missed items per target, 4-alternative then 8-alternative recognition. Target significantly better than Judge; Observer not significantly different from either. Normative data: own FOK G = +.28, peers' average FOK G = +.12, normative probability of recall G = +.38 (Nelson, Leonesio et al. 1986). Calogero (unpublished): given the normative probability, FOK G rose from +.40 to +.58 (norm alone +.55).
limits: Unpublished at the time. Attempts to make people use normative knowledge unaided all failed.
agent_relevance: A base-rate lookup by class (our S0 gate) may beat the model's own feeling of knowing, as the normative probability beat own FOK (.38 vs .28). Supports code-held priors.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: No-Magic Hypothesis: FOK does not read unconscious traces. It uses recallable cues such as acquisition history and partial information, plus rules linking these to the criterion.
numbers: Nelson and Gillespie (unpublished): 16 items learned to one correct recall, 16 to five; retention 3 to 7 weeks. Median FOK 16 for items claimed as recalled five times (actually once) versus 10 for items claimed as once (actually five). FOK correlated with claimed frequency +.40, actual frequency +.23, recognition +.16.
limits: Unpublished. Later work (Koriat 1993, accessibility) both supports and revises it.
agent_relevance: Model self-ratings likely track surface cues (fluency, remembered effort) more than correctness. Predict this and test it: vary the cue, hold correctness fixed.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Monitoring drives control, but weakly and with incomplete compensation. People study items they think are harder longer, yet items judged easier are still recalled better afterwards.
numbers: Nelson and Leonesio (1988): EOL vs study time mean r = -.3; EOL vs recall after self-paced study G = +.48; students told to study until sure of 100% reached 49% recall in Experiment 1. Time vs FOK correlation small in Experiments 2 and 3.
limits: One self-paced trial per item; multi-trial learning not tested here.
agent_relevance: People stop early and under-spend. An LLM budget rule driven by self-rating will under-spend the same way. Our G12 (spend by difficulty) should set the budget from a code-measured signal.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Experimental test of control quality: the experimenter, not the person, set study time using the person's FOK. Giving more time to items judged known was worse; giving more time to items judged unknown was no better than equal or random times.
numbers: n = 52 per group, same total time. Recall 63.9% (constant 4.3 s), 64.5% (random 8 vs .5 s), 64.4% (more time to low FOK), 56.7% (more time to high FOK). The random group showed time mattered (G = +.39 between study time and recall).
limits: Unpublished; two-level time split (8 s vs .5 s) only. Authors suggest a wider spread or better accuracy of EOL/FOK might help.
agent_relevance: A control policy is only as good as the monitor behind it. Extra effort aimed by a weak signal gave zero gain. Gate extra reasoning on a validated signal.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Retrieval timing supports a two-counter FOK. Fast FOK ratings occur at both ends of the scale and slow ones in the middle, so there is a separate quick 'I do not know' signal. FOK latency is shorter than recall latency.
numbers: Schreiber, Nelson and Narens (unpublished), n = 10, 239 questions, 6-point scale. Nonmonotonic latency curve (Fig. 10). Correct-recall latency 2.9 s (FOK 6) to 5.6 s (FOK 1) and always longer than the matching FOK latency.
limits: n = 10, unpublished. Replicates and extends Reder (1987, 1988).
agent_relevance: A cheap fast pre-check ('can I answer this at all?') before spending tokens is a justified control step, and it should have both a yes-evidence and a no-evidence path.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Ongoing FOK controls when search stops on failure, but not when a wrong answer is given. FOK tracks the latency of omission errors but not of commission errors; retrospective confidence tracks latency for both.
numbers: FOK vs omission-error latency G = +.60 (Nelson et al. 1990, replicating Nelson et al. 1984). FOK vs commission latency G = +.03. Confidence vs commission latency G = -.40; confidence vs correct-recall latency G = -.55. Omission latency 20.5 to 25.1 s versus correct 9.8 to 15.2 s (typed); 9.9 s versus 2.9 s (spoken). Reminiscence p = .29 after commission, .05 after omission.
limits: Latency alone does not explain confidence: correct and commission curves differ at 10 to 22 s (Nelson and Calogero, unpublished, 106 questions).
agent_relevance: Two different stop signals exist: 'no answer coming' and 'this answer is good'. Code should keep them apart in S6/S7.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Measurement design. Gamma (Goodman-Kruskal) is used for monitoring accuracy because it needs no distribution assumptions, ignores ties, and its expected value does not depend on the confidence threshold. Resolution (relative) and calibration (absolute) can disagree.
numbers: Lam (1987): between-subject SD of FOK accuracy .36 for rankings versus .41 for ratings; ranking-rating correlation +.71 to +.87. Overconfidence found in normal and alcohol-intoxicated people alike; near-perfect calibration sometimes (Nelson et al. 1990).
limits: Later work (Masson and Rotello 2009) argues gamma can be biased; covered by other subfields. Individual gamma scores are unstable (Nelson 1988).
agent_relevance: For our monitor tests use a rank metric for relative accuracy (AUROC or gamma) and a calibration curve for absolute, and report both.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Practice does not improve FOK accuracy. Feedback on FOK against recognition gave no gain; without feedback there was a small gain in one experiment that did not replicate.
numbers: Experiment 1: 58 with feedback, 58 without, 3 blocks of 15 items: feedback group flat; no-feedback group small rise block 1 to 3, t(57) = 2.69. Experiment 2: n = 36, 4 blocks of 10, no change.
limits: Group-level stability only. Individual scores vary widely.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a model to calibrate by in-context practice alone. Add an outside correction (code-fitted map from raw score to calibrated).

source: Dunlosky and Nelson (1994) Does the sensitivity of judgments of learning to the effects of various study activities depend on when the JOLs occur?
finding: The delayed-JOL effect, first main result: judgments of learning made right after study barely predicted later recall item by item, but judgments made after a delay predicted it very well. Delayed judgments also tracked the effect of the study method on recall.
numbers: Mean gamma between JOL and recall. Experiment 1 (36 students, imagery vs rote): immediate +.10 (imagery), +.29 (rote), overall +.18; delayed +.72 and +.93, overall +.83. Experiment 2 (56 students; distributed, massed, single): immediate +.14, +.12, +.20, overall +.21; delayed +.71, +.83, +.91, overall +.83. Delayed JOL magnitude was higher for imagery than rote, t(35) = 5.92.
limits: Within-subject mixed lists. Explanation is the monitoring-retrieval hypothesis: a delay clears transient short-term information so the judgment must use long-term retrieval. Bjork and others argue delayed JOLs partly reflect covert retrieval practice; Weaver and Kelemen (1997) raise a scale-use artifact (reported in search results, not opened).
agent_relevance: Monitoring a fresh output is inflated by what is still in working context. For our agent: judge a draft after a context reset or with the draft re-read cold, not in the same breath. This is a concrete S4/S8 design lever.

source: Nelson and Dunlosky (1991) When people's judgments of learning are extremely accurate at predicting subsequent recall: the delayed-JOL effect
finding: Original report of the delayed-JOL effect: delayed JOLs were far more accurate than immediate JOLs at predicting recall.
numbers: No numbers read this session. Search summaries only confirm the citation (Psychological Science 2(4), 267-270) and the direction of the effect. See a20 for numbers from the 1994 follow-up.
limits: Not opened. Cited by Dunlosky and Nelson (1994) and the Nelson and Narens (1990) chapter (as unpublished Dunlosky and Nelson).
agent_relevance: Same lever as a20. Treat as unverified until read.

source: Thiede, Anderson and Therriault (2003) Accuracy of metacognitive monitoring affects learning of texts
finding: Better monitoring caused better regulation and better learning. Writing keywords after a delay made comprehension ratings more accurate; those readers then chose weaker texts to reread and scored higher on the final test.
numbers: N = 66 (22 per group), 6 expository texts. Monitoring accuracy differed by group, F(2, 63) = 4.07. Regulation of study, gamma between rating and restudy choice (magnitude): delayed keyword .79, immediate keyword .35, no keyword .36. First test equal across groups (F < 1). Second test higher for delayed group, F(2, 63) = 3.90: old items .69 vs .53 and .56; new items .66 vs .51 and .55. Texts later selected for restudy: first test .27 vs .43 and .44; second test .71 vs .51 and .57. Restudy count did not differ (F(2, 63) = 1.14).
limits: Keyword timing was the lever; it could also change study in other ways. Gamma means for monitoring are shown only in a figure. Sign of the regulation gamma was lost in text extraction; a stronger negative value means better regulation. One lab, university students, short texts. Previous null links between accuracy and memory (Dunlosky and Hertzog) came from comparing age groups.
agent_relevance: This is the cleanest human test that the monitor-to-control link pays off: improve the signal, hold the budget fixed, and outcomes rise. For S6 it says the expected gain from a better monitor is realised only through the choice of what to redo.

source: Metcalfe and Kornell (2003) The dynamics of learning and allocation of study time to a region of proximal learning
finding: Against the dominant discrepancy-reduction model. With free choice people studied the easiest unlearned items first and spent most time on medium items, not the hardest. When time was assigned by the experimenter, spending it on medium items worked best.
numbers: Experiment 1: 12 Columbia students, English-Spanish pairs, time limits 5 s, 15 s and unlimited. Mean time on the hardest items rose 0.71 s, 3.56 s, 8.61 s as limit rose, yet hardest-item recall did not improve; easy and medium items did. Experiment 2 (12 students; 10 s on one class, 1 s on the others): recall .32 emphasise-medium, .27 emphasise-easy, .25 emphasise-difficult, F(2, 22) = 4.39; only medium items gained from extra time, t(11) = 3.89. Literature count (Son and Metcalfe 2000): 35 of 46 conditions in 19 reports showed more time to harder items.
limits: Small samples (12 per experiment). Effect of emphasis lost some significance with stricter scoring (F(4, 44) = 1.90, p = .13 for the interaction). Items were foreign-language pairs, so not obviously general. Authors note no earlier direct test showed that favouring hard items helps.
agent_relevance: A rule such as 'spend most on the hardest case' is not backed by data. Give extra budget to cases that are in reach (some partial progress), and cut it from cases showing no progress. This agrees with our G12 (search only where there is a foothold).

source: Metcalfe and Kornell (2003) The dynamics of learning and allocation of study time to a region of proximal learning
finding: Information-uptake functions explain the medium-item preference: easy items gain a lot in the first fraction of a second and then flatten, medium items keep gaining for longer. A spacing prediction followed: for very short exposures spacing hurt.
numbers: Experiments 3A (33 students) and 3B (29): easy items gained faster only in the first 0 to 0.5 s interval, t(32) = 2.86; medium items gained faster at later intervals, t(32) = 1.82 (second) and 1.75 (last); 3B at 2 to 4 s, t(27) = 2.52. Experiments 4A and 4B (24 each): spacing helped only at 8 s exposure (t(23) = 3.07), no effect at 1 s, and at 0.5 s massing beat spacing.
limits: One-tailed tests in places. Within-subject designs; materials were Spanish-English pairs.
agent_relevance: Gives a shape to use: marginal return per unit effort differs by item and saturates. A stop rule based on measured gain per step (see a26) is better than one based on a fixed budget.

source: Metcalfe and Kornell (2005) A Region of Proximal Learning model of study time allocation
finding: Region of Proximal Learning model. Choice has two steps: drop items judged already known, then study the rest from nearly-known to hard. Perseverance is governed by a different signal: the judged rate of learning (jROL). Keep studying while jROL is high; stop when it nears zero.
numbers: Eight new experiments. Choice among unlearned items: selected items had higher JOL (36.70) than rejected (25.31), t(47) = 4.24; gamma between choice and JOL +.34, t(45) = 4.58. Experiment 7: 42 students, 6 easy, 6 medium, 6 difficult pairs, three study-test cycles; study time rose with lower JOL but tapered at very low JOLs, with long-studiers persisting longer on low-JOL items.
limits: Authors measured jROL crudely as initial JOL minus stopping JOL, not by sampling during study. Unpublished-by-others at the time; later replications not checked here.
agent_relevance: A negative correlation between difficulty and effort is not proof of good control. The model separates 'is it already done' from 'is it moving'. S6 should keep both: a check-pass signal and a progress-rate signal.

source: Metcalfe and Kornell (2005) A Region of Proximal Learning model of study time allocation
finding: Test of the stopping rule: people do not stop when a learned-enough criterion is met. Stop-time JOLs ranged over the whole scale. They stopped on rate of progress, not on level reached.
numbers: Experiment 8: 19 participants, 283 non-negative JOL changes; correlation between change in JOL (initial to stopping) and study time r = .40, p < .0001. Stopping JOLs were spread across the range on trials 2 and 3 (only a small peak at 100 on trial 1). Mean study time per item 11.38 s on list 1 then 8.49, 7.63, 7.18, 6.43 s; final accuracy about .82 on every list. Study time was short for very low and very high stopping JOLs and longest in the midrange.
limits: Correlation, not experiment; jROL was proxied by a two-point difference. N = 19. This result contradicts the 'norm of study' stop rule in Nelson and Narens (1990) Fig. 4 (a05), or at least shows the norm is not a fixed JOL level.
agent_relevance: Key design point for S6: stop an operator when measured gain per attempt falls near zero (code can measure it by test pass counts), not when a confidence number reaches a threshold.

source: Koriat and Goldsmith (1996) Monitoring and control processes in the strategic regulation of memory accuracy
finding: Formal model of monitoring and control for memory reporting. Each best-candidate answer has an assessed probability of being right (Pa). The person volunteers it only if Pa passes a response criterion (Prc) set by the payoff for accuracy. Accuracy and quantity of reported answers then depend on three separable things: retention, monitoring resolution, and control criterion.
numbers: Simulations used 11 probability levels (0 to 1.0). With no resolution (slope 0) free report gives no accuracy gain and only cuts quantity. With good resolution a higher criterion raises accuracy at small quantity cost. Quantity falls faster as the criterion rises.
limits: Normative-style simulation with hypothetical data; the experiments below test only a few cells. Prc was estimated per person from the data.
agent_relevance: This is the cleanest formal template for our abstain-or-answer rule: P(answer) = f(resolution, criterion), and criterion should follow the cost of a wrong answer. Note it conflicts with G6 only when nothing is better; G6 says never abstain on the first pass.

source: Koriat and Goldsmith (1996) Monitoring and control processes in the strategic regulation of memory accuracy
finding: Experiment 1: freedom to withhold answers raised accuracy sharply, and a stricter payoff made people stricter. Accuracy gains came with a quantity loss. People based volunteering almost entirely on their confidence.
numbers: N = 71 Haifa undergraduates, 60-item general-knowledge test, recall or 5-choice recognition, forced phase then free phase, moderate or high accuracy incentive (17 to 19 per cell). Recall: forced accuracy 46.7%; free-report accuracy 76.4% (moderate) and 88.1% (high); free-report quantity 38.0% and 38.5%. Recognition: forced 63.5%; free accuracy 84.4% and 91.1%; quantity 47.3% and 43.6%. Report option effect on accuracy F(1, 32) = 206.82. Volunteered answers had mean confidence .89 versus .29 for withheld. Confidence-volunteering gamma .97 (recall), .93 (recognition); confidence-correctness gamma .87 and .68. ANDI .61 (recall), .30 (recognition). Criterion Prc 65.9 (recall), 79.6 (recognition). Answers volunteered: 26.9 high incentive versus 30.9 moderate.
limits: Table 1 column assignment inferred from layout; consistent with text means of .47 and .64 forced. Same participants did forced then free phase in Experiment 1 (phase order was counterbalanced in Experiment 2). General-knowledge questions in Hebrew.
agent_relevance: Direct human precedent for selective answering with a self-confidence gate: accuracy up by about 30 points at a quantity cost of about 8 points. Also shows people act on confidence almost deterministically (gamma .93 to .97) whether or not it is valid, see a29.

source: Koriat and Goldsmith (1996) Monitoring and control processes in the strategic regulation of memory accuracy
finding: Experiment 2: control only helps if monitoring is valid. On deceptive items where confidence was uninformative, people still used it to decide what to report, and gained almost nothing in accuracy. Retention was the same; the difference was monitoring.
numbers: About 30 participants (df = 28), 90 recall items (30 standard, 30 deceptive, 30 difficult). Standard: forced accuracy 27.9%, free accuracy 75.0%, quantity 22.3%. Deceptive: forced 11.8%, free 21.0%, quantity 7.6%. Accuracy gain 47 points standard vs 9 points deceptive, F(1, 28) = 48.44; quantity cost 6 vs 4 points. Deceptive items: mean confidence .32 against .12 correct; standard .31 against .28. Volunteering gamma with confidence .95 (standard) and .88 (deceptive). Matched-standard subtest (27 participants): free accuracy 63.0%, quantity 8.6%.
limits: Standard and deceptive sets differ in difficulty; the authors built a matched-standard set to check and the conclusion held. Numbers for N inferred from degrees of freedom.
agent_relevance: Strongest single result for our 'code monitors, model acts' choice: a confident but wrong monitor still controls behaviour. If the model's self-confidence is the gate, misleading items defeat the whole scheme. Use a code check as the gate.

source: Koriat (1997) Monitoring one's own knowledge during study: a cue-utilization approach to judgments of learning
finding: Cue-utilization account of JOLs. People judge learning from three cue types: intrinsic (item difficulty), extrinsic (conditions such as repetition and exposure time), and mnemonic (feel of how well it is known). They lean on intrinsic cues and discount extrinsic ones. Practice shifts the basis toward mnemonic cues and improves resolution while hurting calibration.
numbers: Experiment 1: 50 Hebrew pairs, two study-test blocks, 16 participants per condition (Same list twice vs Different lists). Mean recall 67.2 vs mean JOL 55.5 (underconfidence). JOL-recall gamma rose from .58 to .67 (Same) and .59 to .65 (Different), presentation effect F(1, 30) = 4.28, p < .05. Repetition lifted recall more than JOL.
limits: Cued paired associates; four experiments in total, only Experiment 1 read in detail. This conflicts with Nelson and Narens (1990) on one point: they found no learning-to-learn gain for FOK (a19), while Koriat found gains for JOL resolution. Different judgment types.
agent_relevance: Support for the No-Magic idea (a13): self-ratings come from cues, not direct trace reading. For an LLM: rating shifts with surface cues such as problem length or phrasing. Calibrate per cue type, and expect extrinsic factors (retries, hints) to be under-weighted.

source: Callaway, Griffiths, Norman and Zhang (2023) Optimal metacognitive control of memory recall
finding: Formal rational model of Nelson and Narens' retrieval control. Search for a memory is a process whose progress is monitored; the meta level stops it when the expected value of continuing falls below its cost, and reports a feeling of knowing from the inferred strength. Two preregistered experiments confirm the key predictions, with objective strength measured before the critical trials.
numbers: Experiment 1: 612 recruited on Prolific; participants were faster to recall high-confidence targets (B = -0.244, t(516.1) = -9.54) and slower to give up on targets with high feeling of knowing (B = 0.385, t(189.1) = 10.02), replicating Costermans et al. (1992). Using pretest accuracy as an objective strength, people were faster to recall strong targets (B = -0.978, t(253.3) = -8.11) and slower to skip them. Experiment 2: 685 recruited, 184 excluded, 501 analysed, two cues per trial; gaze time on stronger cue B = 0.187, t(326.9) = 41.46; final fixations longer than non-final; probability of fixating the weaker memory fell with fixation length (B = -1.376, z = -16.78).
limits: Online Prolific samples with large exclusions in Experiment 2 (27%). Model fit was described as moderate quantitative. Authors changed the lesioned-model fitting after seeing data in Experiment 2, and say so. Cue-recall of image pairs, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: Gives a computational form of the 'stop searching' rule that we can copy: continue while expected gain exceeds cost, switch targets when another looks stronger. It is a value-of-computation rule that code can run. Matches a16 and a17.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Early test of monitoring in language models. Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions when the format is right. A model asked 'is your proposed answer true?' (P(True)) separates its correct from incorrect samples, and improves when shown several of its own samples first. A head trained to predict whether the model knows the answer (P(IK)) works in distribution but transfers unevenly.
numbers: 52B model. P(IK) AUROC and Brier, trained on TriviaQA only: TriviaQA .864/.151, arithmetic .928/.194, LAMBADA .606/.431, Python synthesis .687/.164, GSM8K .624/.200. Trained on all tasks except GSM8K: .873/.145, .987/.042, .853/.108, .881/.109, GSM8K .752/.121. Replacing an option with 'none of the above' hurt performance and calibration. RLHF policies looked miscalibrated but one temperature change (T = 2.5) largely repaired it.
limits: Columns of the table assigned from the layout. Accuracy filtered by P(True) > 0.5 was higher than base accuracy, gap growing with size, but exact figures are in figures only. 2022 models; P(IK) training needs finetuning and is not available to a prompt-only scaffold. The model has no way to know which tokens it wrote.
agent_relevance: Self-evaluation after proposing is a usable monitor but weak out of distribution (AUROC near .6 on new task types). Do not trust it on a class never measured; fit or check it on our own tasks (G7).

source: Oh and Gobet (2025) Monitor-Generate-Verify (MGV): formalising metacognitive theory for language model reasoning
finding: Monitor-Generate-Verify (MGV) is a computational translation of Flavell and Nelson and Narens for language-model reasoning. It adds a monitoring step before generation (difficulty and confidence) that is updated from verification feedback. It keeps the norm-of-study formula, dual-counter FOK and satisficing threshold. The paper presents no empirical test.
numbers: Cites a 'prefix dominance trap' of roughly 20% accuracy loss when a model commits to a poor strategy early (taken from Luo et al. 2025, not checked). Worked example: target 90% performance with 20% decay needs 108% mastery during acquisition (values over 100% show the formula is only a sketch). Appendix links to resource-rational models: strategy selection as a bandit (Lieder and Griffiths 2017), planning as a meta-level MDP (Callaway 2022), memory recall (Callaway 2023, see a31).
limits: Authors say: no empirical validation and no normative justification for the design choices. A vocabulary paper, not evidence of benefit.
agent_relevance: Useful as a checklist for which Nelson-Narens parts our S6 lacks (pre-generation monitor, learned monitor update). Weight it as a design idea only (status [D]).

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs know when they know, but do not act on it: a metacognitive harness for test-time scaling
finding: Direct engineering test of the Nelson-Narens split in an LLM harness. A fixed Claude Sonnet 4.6 reports a pre-solve feeling of knowing (FOK) and a post-solve judgment of learning (JOL); a small learned classifier (not the model) turns the two numbers into stop, retry or aggregate decisions. The paper reports the model has the signals but does not use them to steer its own effort.
numbers: Pooled 1,859 test items: accuracy 48.3 to 56.9 (+8.6); HLE subset 48.0 to 60.0. Anchor set N = 100, accuracy .58: FOK AUROC .612, JOL AUROC .745, joint AUROC .757. Ablation on 100 items (Pass@1 44.0%, Oracle@4 53.0%): full 47.0 [37, 57], avg 2.58 attempts; no FOK 45.0; no JOL 42.0; hand-tuned (1-JOL) times FOK 42.0; random retry at matched K 45.7 [43, 48]; last-answer 40.0; max-JOL 44.0; feeding full previous reasoning 40.0.
limits: Preprint, one base model for the main gain. The ablation intervals overlap heavily; control beats random retry at matched budget by only 1.3 points on 100 items. Reasoning length did not follow confidence in a consistent way across nine models. Leaderboard comparisons use public snapshots.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our S6: code decides, model reports signals. Learned thresholds beat hand-set ones in the ablation. Passing prior reasoning back hurt (40.0 vs 47.0), which supports our fresh-context rule in S3.

source: Mazzoni and Cornoldi (1993) When can people allocate study time effectively? Labor-in-vain
finding: Reported through a search summary only: items studied longest were often not recalled better than items studied briefly (labor in vain). It did not vanish with the manipulations tried and disappeared only when time was experimenter-paced.
numbers: No numbers read. Summary says the effect was not due to inability to manage study time (Experiment 3).
limits: Not opened. Summary comes from a search snippet; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Warns that more effort on a case does not guarantee a better result; matches a14 and a23.

source: Rhodes and Tauber (2011) The influence of delaying judgments of learning on metacognitive accuracy: a meta-analytic review
finding: Meta-analysis of the delayed-JOL effect (Psychological Bulletin 137, 131-148). Not opened. A search snippet from a later review mentions 98 effect sizes and only a small benefit of delay on recall (g = 0.08); that line is about recall, not accuracy, and is unverified.
numbers: No accuracy figures confirmed this session.
limits: Not opened. A conflict check on a20 still has to be done from the paper itself.
agent_relevance: Treat a20 as a lab-condition result until the meta-analysis is read.
